title: BroadcastReceivers & ContentProviders
scopeHtml: Scope: receiver registration and delivery rules, export/security flags, ordered/sticky/local broadcasts, goAsync, ContentProvider mechanics, FileProvider, provider init order, URI permissions. Intent/PendingIntent internals are chunk 10; Doze/alarm behavior is chunk 17.

notes.title: BroadcastReceiver registration and dynamic receiver leaks
notes.html:
The idea. A broadcast is a message the system or an app shouts to everyone ("battery low", "screen off", "network changed"). A BroadcastReceiver is the object that listens. There are two ways to register one.

  • Manifest-declared: <receiver> with an <intent-filter>. The system can start your process to deliver it. Since Android 8.0 (API 26) most implicit broadcasts no longer work this way (see the next section).
  • Context-registered (dynamic): registerReceiver(receiver, filter) while a component is alive. You get broadcasts only while registered, and you must unregister.
private val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { /* main thread, ~10 s limit */ }
}
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    ContextCompat.registerReceiver(this, receiver,
        IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_LOW), ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED)
}
override fun onStop() { unregisterReceiver(receiver); super.onStop() }

Match registration and unregistration to symmetric lifecycle pairs: onCreate/onDestroy, onStart/onStop or onResume/onPause. onReceive runs on the main thread by default (or the Handler you pass); a receiver object is valid only during onReceive (do not bind to a service from a manifest receiver, and do not use it as a long-lived object).

Dynamic receiver leak (spot-the-bug). Registering in onCreate with no unregister, or registering in onResume without unregistering in onPause (calling registerReceiver multiple times accumulates duplicates when the Activity returns). Logcat shows Activity ... has leaked IntentReceiver ... that was originally registered here. Are you missing a call to unregisterReceiver()?, and LeakCanary shows ActivityThread -> mAllApplicationReceivers/ReceiverDispatcher -> receiver -> Activity. Unregistering twice throws IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered. Registering with the Application context from an Activity-bound inner class leaks the Activity for the life of the process.

Real products. Network-aware apps (Gmail, WhatsApp) once used CONNECTIVITY_ACTION receivers; today they use ConnectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback. Music apps register for ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY dynamically while playing.

Analogy. A manifest receiver is a phone number listed in a directory (the system may wake you). A dynamic receiver is you standing at a bus stop with your hand raised: it only works while you stand there, and you must put your hand down.

Common interview traps.

  • Registering in onCreate and unregistering in onStop (asymmetric: second visit doesn't register again).
  • Doing long work in onReceive.
  • Thinking a manifest-declared receiver stays in memory between broadcasts.

notes.title: Implicit broadcast limits
notes.html:
The idea. In Android 8.0 (API 26) Google stopped apps from waking up for most broadcasts they did not need, because dozens of apps starting for every CONNECTIVITY_ACTION drained the battery and memory.

Rules.

  • An explicit broadcast targets a specific component/package, so it still works.
  • An implicit broadcast (no specific target) may not be received by manifest-declared receivers in apps targeting API 26+, with an exception list: ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED, ACTION_LOCALE_CHANGED, ACTION_MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, ACTION_TIMEZONE_CHANGED, SMS/MMS ones, ACTION_USB_*, ACTION_HEADSET_PLUG, some NEW_OUTGOING_CALL, and others (see the "Implicit broadcast exceptions" doc).
  • Dynamic receivers still receive implicit broadcasts while registered.
  • Android 7.0 (API 24) had already removed manifest CONNECTIVITY_ACTION and picture/video broadcasts (ACTION_NEW_PICTURE, ACTION_NEW_VIDEO).

Alternatives. NetworkCallback for connectivity, JobScheduler/WorkManager constraints (NetworkType, charging, idle), ACTION_POWER_CONNECTED replaced with Constraints.setRequiresCharging, PackageManager change listeners, FCM for server events, AlarmManager for time.

Production incident. After raising targetSdk to 26+, a feature that "sync when plugged in" via a manifest ACTION_POWER_CONNECTED receiver silently stops for all users; no crash, just missing analytics. Fix: WorkManager with a charging constraint.

Real products. WhatsApp and Facebook moved from connectivity receivers to JobScheduler/WorkManager; Android's own docs list broadcasts that were migrated.

Analogy. A hotel stopped paging every guest for every announcement; only emergency alarms (the exempt list) still ring every room, everything else is on the lobby board for people who are present.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the restriction is based on the device API level; it is based on targetSdkVersion (for most background restrictions the app's target, with some system-wide).
  • Thinking explicit broadcasts are restricted too.
  • Not knowing dynamic registration is an allowed fallback while the app is alive.

notes.title: Exported flags, RECEIVER_EXPORTED and exported component security
notes.html:
The idea. An exported component can be started or called by other apps. An unexported one is private. If you export something by mistake, any app on the phone may trigger it.

Manifest rules.

  • android:exported is mandatory for any component with an intent filter when targeting Android 12 (API 31): the build fails or install is rejected if missing.
  • Components without intent filters default to not exported; with a filter they used to default to exported. Always write it explicitly.
  • Exported components should be protected with a permission (signature level for your own apps) or validate the caller (getCallingUid(), Binder.getCallingUid, checkCallingPermission).

Dynamic receivers on Android 13/14. On apps targeting API 34 (Android 14), registerReceiver for non-system broadcasts must state a flag: RECEIVER_EXPORTED (other apps may send) or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED (only your app and the system), otherwise SecurityException: ... One of RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts. ContextCompat.registerReceiver supplies the flag on older versions as well.

PendingIntent mutability. Android 12 requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE on PendingIntents; an implicit mutable PendingIntent lets other apps rewrite the action. Android 14 forbids mutable implicit PendingIntents.

Common vulnerabilities.

  • Exported Activity that takes a URL extra and loads it in a WebView with JavaScript: other apps can inject content (intent redirection / WebView attack).
  • Exported receiver that performs a sensitive action (reset password, start recording) on an unauthenticated broadcast.
  • Exported provider returning data without permission checks (SQL injection / path traversal).
  • Launching an Intent you extracted from an incoming extra (intent.getParcelableExtra("next") then startActivity): intent redirection allows reaching your non-exported components.

Real products. Google Play's pre-launch report and security checks (and tools like Android Lint, MobSF) flag exported components; many public bug bounty reports (Samsung, TikTok, banking apps) were exported components.

Analogy. Exported = a door facing the street; if it opens onto the stock room with no lock, anyone can walk in.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving out android:exported on Android 12+ targets.
  • Thinking RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED blocks system broadcasts; it does not.
  • Using a normal-level permission to protect a sensitive component instead of signature.

notes.title: Ordered, sticky and local broadcasts, and LocalBroadcastManager migration
notes.html:
Ordered broadcasts. sendOrderedBroadcast delivers to one receiver at a time in priority order (android:priority from -1000 to 1000). A receiver can modify the result (setResultData) or stop the chain (abortBroadcast()). Useful for "first handler wins" (old SMS interception flow). Still works but is restricted for system ones; priority is only meaningful among receivers with the same filter and mostly ignored for dynamic vs manifest ordering (dynamic registered ones are delivered first, in the ordered case manifest ones last).

Sticky broadcasts. sendStickyBroadcast kept the last Intent around so a later registerReceiver returned it immediately. Deprecated since API 21 because they are insecure (no permission on the receiving side) and slow. The remaining legitimate use is reading system sticky state: registerReceiver(null, IntentFilter(ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED)) returns the current battery Intent without registering a receiver.

Local broadcasts. LocalBroadcastManager (AndroidX) kept messages inside your process: faster and private. It is deprecated (androidx.localbroadcastmanager 1.1.0) because it is an app-wide event bus with no lifecycle awareness and is easy to misuse.

Migration under live traffic.

  1. List every local action and its sender/receivers.
  2. Replace with a typed in-process channel: a SharedFlow/StateFlow in a repository or a LiveData, scoped by DI (Hilt singleton); collect with repeatOnLifecycle.
  3. Keep both paths during a transition release (dual emission) if third-party modules still listen.
  4. Cross-process messages become explicit: bound service/AIDL, ContentObserver, or setPackage() explicit broadcasts.
  5. Add tests for lifecycle re-subscription (a SharedFlow with replay = 0 loses events when no collector is active; use replay, a Channel, or persisted state when events must not be lost).
object Events { val refresh = MutableSharedFlow<Unit>(extraBufferCapacity = 1) }
// sender:  Events.refresh.tryEmit(Unit)
// receiver: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { Events.refresh.collect { reload() } } }

Real products. Many large codebases (Twitter, Airbnb) moved to Flow/event bus abstractions or Redux-style state; Firebase Messaging uses explicit service callbacks.

Analogy. Ordered broadcast is a relay where each runner can stop the baton; sticky is a notice-board that remembers the last notice; local is an internal office intercom.

Common interview traps.

  • Using sticky broadcasts for your own app state.
  • Thinking LocalBroadcastManager sends across processes (it doesn't).
  • Replacing with a SharedFlow and losing events when no collector exists.

notes.title: goAsync and receiver timeouts, and the receiver ANR
notes.html:
The idea. onReceive is a main-thread callback and the system gives it very little time: the process is considered "busy" and an ANR timer is running. When onReceive returns, the receiver is finished, and the system may kill the process because nothing else is keeping it alive.

Timeouts. About 10 seconds for foreground broadcasts, 60 seconds for background ones (confirm in docs). Exceeding it produces Broadcast of Intent { ... } ... ANR ("Context.startForegroundService did not then call Service.startForeground" is a different error). Even before the timeout, a slow receiver delays other broadcast dispatching for that queue.

goAsync(). Calling val pending = goAsync() tells the system "I am not finished when onReceive returns". You do the work on another thread and call pending.finish(). It still runs under the same ~10 s limit, only moving work off the main thread; it does not make a long task safe. For anything longer: start a foreground service (only if allowed), or enqueue WorkManager.

override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) {
    val pending = goAsync()
    CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default).launch {
        try { quickWrite(i) } finally { pending.finish() }   // must always finish
    }
}

Forgetting finish() leaves the broadcast stuck until the timeout and may ANR.

Receiver ANR (production incident). Crashlytics shows Executing service ... or Broadcast of Intent { act=android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED } with a main-thread stack in a database open or network call in onReceive. Causes: disk I/O on a cold process at boot (device is slow right after boot), synchronous network, lock contention. Fixes: do only trivial work in onReceive, hand off to WorkManager, goAsync for short async work, keep Application.onCreate light (it runs first for a cold process, and its time counts against the receiver).

Real products. SMS apps and payment OTP apps (Paytm, PhonePe) use goAsync for small parsing and then post a notification or schedule work.

Analogy. A restaurant waiter told "take this order to the kitchen and be back in 10 seconds", not "go cook the meal".

Common interview traps.

  • Believing goAsync extends the deadline.
  • Starting a thread from onReceive without goAsync (the process may die).
  • Forgetting Application.onCreate time adds to receiver time on cold start.

notes.title: BOOT_COMPLETED
notes.html:
The idea. After the phone reboots, apps can ask to be told so they can reschedule work (alarms and jobs are cleared at reboot). The broadcast is ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED.

Requirements.

  • Permission RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED in the manifest.
  • A manifest receiver (this is on the implicit-broadcast exception list).
  • Credential-encrypted storage is not available until the user unlocks the device after reboot (file-based encryption). Use ACTION_LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED with android:directBootAware="true" and device-protected storage if you need to run before first unlock (alarm apps).
  • The app must not be in stopped state: a freshly installed app never launched, or force-stopped, gets no broadcasts until the user opens it once.

Production incident ("reminders don't fire after reboot"). Causes: missing permission, receiver not exported/declared, user force-stopped, OEM auto-start restrictions (Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo require "autostart" settings), doing heavy work in the receiver (ANR at boot while the system is busy), or Android 15 limits on starting some foreground service types from BOOT_COMPLETED. Fix: re-enqueue WorkManager (WorkManager reschedules itself after reboot automatically), reset alarms in the receiver quickly, test with adb reboot, and use adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED -p pkg for quick checks.

Real products. Alarm clocks (Google Clock), calendar reminders, VPN apps and fitness apps reschedule on boot; WorkManager's RescheduleReceiver does it for you.

Analogy. After a power cut, the building manager rings each shop to say "power is back, restart your fridges" but never calls a shop whose key was never handed in (stopped-state app).

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting BOOT_COMPLETED before the user unlocks (use the locked variant with Direct Boot).
  • Forgetting the permission or the exported attribute on Android 12+.
  • Doing a lot of work at boot instead of enqueueing a job.

notes.title: ContentProvider basics and alternatives
notes.html:
The idea. A ContentProvider is a standard "front desk" for data. Other components or apps ask for data through a URI like content://com.example.notes/notes/5, and the provider answers, usually with a Cursor. It also lets the system apply permissions and observe changes.

Operations. query, insert, update, delete, getType, plus call for custom methods. Access is through ContentResolver. Callers use URIs; UriMatcher maps a URI to a table/row.

class NotesProvider : ContentProvider() {
    override fun onCreate(): Boolean { db = NotesDb(context!!); return true }   // keep fast!
    override fun query(uri: Uri, proj: Array<String>?, sel: String?, args: Array<String>?, order: String?): Cursor? =
        db.readableDatabase.query("notes", proj, sel, args, null, null, order)
            .also { it.setNotificationUri(context!!.contentResolver, uri) }
    /* insert, update, delete, getType ... */
}

Binder threads handle the calls (a pool), not the main thread, so providers must be thread-safe. In the same process the call is direct (no Binder); across processes it is an IPC transaction.

When to use a provider. Sharing data with other apps (Contacts, MediaStore, Calendar, Downloads/Documents via SAF DocumentsProvider), supporting system features that require one (SyncAdapter, search suggestions, FileProvider, Share sheet), or cross-process access to a database. For app-internal data, a provider is overkill.

Alternatives. Room/DataStore plus a repository (same process), bound service/AIDL (RPC), WorkManager (background), FileProvider (share a file), Intent extras (small), ContentObserver + Flow wrappers; Room with enableMultiInstanceInvalidation for multi-process.

Real products. Android system providers: ContactsContract, MediaStore (Google Photos queries images), CalendarContract, Telephony; Firebase and AndroidX Startup use "hidden" providers (FirebaseInitProvider, InitializationProvider) as auto-init hooks.

Analogy. A library desk: you do not walk into the stacks, you hand a request slip with an address and the librarian decides what to give you, applying the rules.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating a provider just to move data inside one process.
  • Forgetting that provider methods run on Binder threads.
  • Returning a raw SQL exception or unsanitised selection from query (injection).

notes.title: Provider initialization order
notes.html:
The idea. ContentProviders are created very early, before Application.onCreate. That is why libraries use them to auto-initialise without any code from you.

Order in a new process (ActivityThread.handleBindApplication).

  1. Application object instantiated; attachBaseContext(...).
  2. installContentProviders: each declared provider is instantiated and onCreate() called, in order of android:initOrder (higher first) within the process.
  3. Application.onCreate().
  4. Components (Activity, Service, Receiver) start.
attachBaseContext -> provider.attachInfo/onCreate (all) -> Application.onCreate -> Activity

Consequences: a provider's onCreate cannot assume the Application is initialised (DI, Timber, crash SDK not yet ready); getContext() is valid but getApplicationContext() may be partially set up; slow providers delay the whole cold start; a crash in a provider onCreate crashes the process before your crash handler is set (Crashlytics itself initialises via a provider, hence "no crash report" for early crashes). Providers run in each process, so a multi-process app initialises them multiple times unless you set android:process or multiprocess appropriately.

Startup cost fix. Use Jetpack App Startup: it replaces many library providers by a single InitializationProvider that runs Initializers in dependency order; you can remove (tools:node="remove") individual initializers and trigger them lazily with AppInitializer.getInstance(ctx).initializeComponent(...). Measure with Perfetto: ContentProvider.onCreate slices before bindApplication ends.

Real products. Firebase, WorkManager, Emoji2, ProfileInstaller and LeakCanary (older versions) each shipped a provider; apps with 10+ library providers saw tens of ms cumulatively on cold start.

Analogy. Staff arrive and open their small booths (providers) before the shop manager (Application) gives the morning briefing.

Common interview traps.

  • Using application-level singletons inside a provider's onCreate.
  • Believing Application.onCreate is the first code to run in the process.
  • Forgetting providers add to every process's startup.

notes.title: FileProvider and file exposure
notes.html:
The idea. Since Android 7 (API 24), apps may not give other apps a file:// URI: it throws FileUriExposedException. Instead you share content:// URIs produced by androidx.core.content.FileProvider, a special ContentProvider that maps a private file to a safe, temporary-permission URI.

Setup.

<provider android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.fileprovider"
    android:exported="false" android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS" android:resource="@xml/file_paths"/>
</provider>
<paths><files-path name="shared" path="shared/"/></paths>   <!-- only this subfolder -->
val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(ctx, "${ctx.packageName}.fileprovider", file)
val send = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
    type = "image/jpeg"; putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)       // temporary read grant
}
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(send, null))

Exposure bug (spot-the-bug / security review). The XML path config uses <root-path name="all" path=""/> or <external-path path="."/>/<files-path path=""/> which exposes the whole directory (databases, shared preferences, tokens). Any app that gets a grant (or a bug that lets it pick the URI) can read private data. Also: exported="true" on the FileProvider (throws on newer FileProvider versions), grantUriPermissions combined with global permissions, granting write access with FLAG_GRANT_WRITE_URI_PERMISSION unnecessarily, and trusting a filename coming from the caller. Fix: expose only dedicated subfolders (e.g. files/shared/, cache/share/), keep read-only grants, revoke grants with revokeUriPermission when done, and review file_paths.xml in code review. Grant to a specific package via grantUriPermission(pkg, uri, flags) when you know the target.

Camera example. ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE with EXTRA_OUTPUT must be a FileProvider URI; use ActivityResultContracts.TakePicture which handles grants.

Real products. WhatsApp's share-image-to-other-app, Gmail attachments, Google Photos sharing and every camera flow use FileProvider; Android Lint and AppSec scanners check for root-path.

Analogy. Instead of giving a visitor your house key (file path), you give a single-use pass for one specific cupboard.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring root-path or an empty path.
  • Forgetting FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION, so the target app gets SecurityException.
  • Setting exported="true" on FileProvider.

notes.title: Provider permissions and URI grants, and a provider security audit
notes.html:
The idea. A provider can control who may read or write at three levels: whole provider, per-path, and per-URI (temporary grants).

Manifest controls.

  • android:permission (both), android:readPermission, android:writePermission for the provider.
  • <path-permission android:pathPrefix="/private" android:readPermission="..."/> for sub-paths.
  • android:exported (false by default for API 17+ when targeting it; set explicitly).
  • android:grantUriPermissions="true" (all URIs) or <grant-uri-permission android:pathPattern=.../> for specific ones.

URI permission grants. The owner can grant another app temporary access to one URI: Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION (and write) on an Intent carrying the URI as data, ClipData, or EXTRA_STREAM; or context.grantUriPermission(pkg, uri, flags). The grant lasts until the receiving task/Activity finishes (or revokeUriPermission; FLAG_GRANT_PERSISTABLE_URI_PERMISSION plus takePersistableUriPermission for SAF). Android 11+ package visibility affects whether the other app is visible for grantUriPermission.

Audit checklist (post-incident).

  1. Is each provider needed? Remove unused ones.
  2. exported false unless required; if true, require a signature-level permission or per-URI grants.
  3. Use selection arguments (? placeholders), never concatenate: SQL injection in query.
  4. In openFile, canonicalise the path and check it stays inside the allowed directory (path traversal with ../).
  5. Validate Binder.getCallingUid() for sensitive operations; check getCallingPackage().
  6. Never return sensitive columns by default (limit projection).
  7. Review grantUriPermissions and FileProvider paths.
  8. Add automated lint and manual pen tests (Drozer, MobSF).

Production incident pattern. A fintech app's exported provider with no permission and a query building SQL from the selection string exposed user transactions to any installed app; discovered via a bug bounty. Fix: unexport, parameterise queries, add signature permission, rotate data, notify.

Real products. MediaStore enforces scoped access; Gmail grants temporary read to attachments via URI grants; Google's Security Rewards program has paid for exported provider vulnerabilities.

Analogy. A bank vault with a guard (provider permission), separate rooms with their own keys (path permissions), and one-day visitor passes (URI grants) that expire when the visitor leaves.

Common interview traps.

  • Concatenating selection strings.
  • Assuming a URI grant is permanent.
  • Leaving the provider exported "because the library docs showed it".
  • Not checking canonical paths in openFile.

notes.title: ContentObserver and Cursor transport
notes.html:
The idea. Querying a provider returns a Cursor. Because the data may be in another process, the Cursor is not the database itself; it is a window onto a copy, and you can ask to be told when the data changes.

Cursor transport. For cross-process queries the provider returns a CursorWindow backed by shared memory (ashmem): the provider fills rows into a window (default size 2 MB per window), and the client reads from it via CursorToBulkCursorAdaptor / BulkCursorToCursorAdaptor. When you read beyond the window, the client asks the provider to refill a new window using Binder calls. Consequences: very large rows (images in BLOBs) cause SQLiteBlobTooBigException: Row too big to fit into CursorWindow; large result sets are slow; each Binder transaction is limited to about 1 MB, so the data itself goes through shared memory, not through the Parcel. Always close() cursors (use { }) or you leak the window (logcat: Cursor window leaked, Finalizing a Cursor that has not been deactivated or closed).

ContentObserver. Register to learn about changes without polling.

val observer = object : ContentObserver(Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())) {
    override fun onChange(selfChange: Boolean, uri: Uri?) { reload() }
}
contentResolver.registerContentObserver(MediaStore.Images.Media.EXTERNAL_CONTENT_URI, true, observer)
// later
contentResolver.unregisterContentObserver(observer)

The provider calls contentResolver.notifyChange(uri, null) after writes; cursor.setNotificationUri(resolver, uri) makes CursorLoader/cursor adapters auto-refresh. notifyForDescendants=true includes child URIs. Notifications may be coalesced and can arrive in bursts, so debounce. Unregister to avoid leaks (observer holds a Handler and context).

Real products. Gallery and Photos apps observe MediaStore to refresh after a camera shot; contacts and SMS apps observe ContactsContract/Telephony providers; Room's InvalidationTracker is a similar in-process idea.

Analogy. Photocopying a page from a book in the library's own copier (the Cursor window); a doorbell that rings when the book is updated (ContentObserver).

Common interview traps.

  • Not closing Cursors.
  • Storing big blobs in rows and hitting the CursorWindow limit.
  • Assuming onChange carries the exact changed row; often only the parent URI.
  • Forgetting to unregister observers.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Register receivers symmetrically; manifest receivers cannot get most implicit broadcasts since API 26, so use dynamic receivers, WorkManager constraints or callbacks.
  • Declare android:exported explicitly; pick RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED on Android 14 targets; protect exported components with signature permissions and validate callers.
  • Ordered broadcasts chain receivers; sticky is deprecated; LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated: migrate to Flow-based events and mind lost-event semantics.
  • onReceive has about 10 s (foreground) and is on the main thread; goAsync moves work off-thread but not past the deadline.
  • BOOT_COMPLETED needs the permission, an unstopped app and unlocked storage (or Direct Boot); do minimal work and re-enqueue.
  • Providers are created before Application.onCreate; use App Startup to control cost.
  • FileProvider shares content:// URIs: restrict paths, use read grants, never root-path.
  • Secure providers with permissions, parameterised queries, canonical path checks, and short-lived URI grants; close Cursors and unregister ContentObservers.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a manifest-declared receiver and a context-registered receiver, and how do you choose between them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know receiver lifetime and the post-API-26 delivery restrictions, not just the syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A manifest receiver is declared statically, so the system can create my process and deliver a broadcast even if the app is not running. A context-registered receiver lives only while the registering component lives, so I must call registerReceiver and unregisterReceiver. Since API 26 most implicit broadcasts can only reach context-registered receivers, so I default to dynamic registration and keep manifest receivers for the small exempt list like BOOT_COMPLETED or for explicit broadcasts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A receiver is just a callback object: the system calls onReceive(Context, Intent) on the main thread of your process (unless you pass a Handler to registerReceiver).

Manifest receiver                      Context-registered receiver
-------------------------------------  ---------------------------------
Declared in AndroidManifest.xml        registerReceiver() at runtime
Survives with no process: system       Exists only while the registering
  starts your process to deliver       Context is alive and registered
New instance per broadcast             Same instance every time
Subject to API 26+ implicit limits     Not restricted by those limits
Context in onReceive = ReceiverRestrictedContext (cannot bindService,
  cannot registerReceiver with null receiver)

Choose by need: "I only care while my UI/service is up" (connectivity UI banner, battery indicator) means dynamic. "I must wake the app" (boot, package replaced, an explicit broadcast from my own alarm) means manifest. For a manifest receiver the process is started cold, so Application.onCreate runs first, which is a hidden cost of every delivery.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) { /* update UI */ }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        ContextCompat.registerReceiver(
            this, receiver, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_POWER_CONNECTED),
            ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED
        )
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        unregisterReceiver(receiver) // symmetric with onStart, or you leak the Activity
        super.onStop()
    }
}
<receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/>
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Registering in onCreate and unregistering in onDestroy: while stopped the Activity still receives and does UI work; and onDestroy is not guaranteed.
  • Unregistering twice or never: IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered or a leaked Activity (IntentReceiverLeaked in logcat).
  • Doing long work in onReceive; it runs on the main thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a manifest receiver bind to a service? → No, its Context is a restricted one; bindService throws ReceiverCallNotAllowedException. Start a service or enqueue work instead.
  2. Is a receiver instance reused for manifest receivers? → No, a new instance per broadcast, so do not keep state in fields.
  3. How do you register from a Fragment safely? → Use viewLifecycleOwner or DefaultLifecycleObserver onStart/onStop so registration pairs with visibility, not the Fragment object lifetime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "manifest is static, dynamic is runtime". Senior adds the API 26 implicit limit, cold-process cost per delivery, restricted receiver context, lifecycle pairing, and that exported flags are mandatory in both forms on newer targets (see Q176).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A manifest receiver for connectivity changes cold-started the process on every flap, which showed up as a spike in cold-start counts and battery drain; moving to a dynamic registration (and later NetworkCallback) removed it.

questions.promptHtml: What is a ContentProvider, how does a client talk to it, and what does a content URI look like?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates have only used Room and never understood the provider model that FileProvider, MediaStore and contacts are built on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ContentProvider is a component that exposes structured data behind a URI and a CRUD-like interface (query, insert, update, delete, getType). Clients never get the provider object, they use ContentResolver with a content://authority/path/id URI. The call crosses a Binder boundary, so it works across processes and apps, and access is controlled by manifest permissions and URI grants.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
content://com.example.notes.provider/notes/42
\_____/  \______________________/ \____/ \_/
scheme        authority            path   id (optional)
  • The authority is globally unique (reverse-domain by convention). PackageManager maps authority to provider at install time, so two apps with the same authority conflict (INSTALL_FAILED_CONFLICTING_PROVIDER).
  • ContentResolver.query() finds the provider via the system's ActivityManager, gets an IContentProvider Binder proxy, and calls it. If the provider's process is not running, the system starts it (this can be expensive).
  • Cursor results are transferred through a shared-memory CursorWindow (about 2 MB by default per window), not through the 1 MB Binder buffer, but huge rows still fail.
  • UriMatcher maps URI shapes to codes inside the provider; getType returns MIME types (vnd.android.cursor.dir/... for lists, .item/ for single rows).
  • Provider methods are called on Binder threads, not the main thread, so they must be thread-safe. onCreate is the exception: it runs on the main thread during process start, so it must be fast.
  • From Android 11 (API 30), if you target 30+ and need to reach another app's provider you may need <queries><provider android:authority="..."/></queries> for resolution by authority.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val projection = arrayOf(Contacts._ID, Contacts.DISPLAY_NAME)
contentResolver.query(Contacts.CONTENT_URI, projection, null, null, null)?.use { c ->
    val nameIdx = c.getColumnIndexOrThrow(Contacts.DISPLAY_NAME)
    while (c.moveToNext()) println(c.getString(nameIdx))
}
<provider
    android:name=".NotesProvider"
    android:authorities="com.example.notes.provider"
    android:exported="false" />

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting use {} on the Cursor (leaked cursor/CursorWindow).
  • Querying on the main thread; a provider in another process may need to cold start.
  • Assuming a provider is needed for in-app data. Inside one app, it is overhead; use a repository.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a provider exported=false by default? → For targetSdk 17+ the default is false; before that it was true, a historic data leak source.
  2. How do clients observe changes? → Provider calls notifyChange(uri); clients use ContentObserver or the cursor's setNotificationUri (see Q187).
  3. What thread do provider methods run on? → Binder pool threads (or the caller's thread for same-process calls), so guard shared state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can read contacts via ContentResolver. Senior explains authority registration, Binder and CursorWindow transport, thread model, and when not to build a provider at all (Q190).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A same-process "provider for convenience" with a slow onCreate (opening a database) added 80 ms to every cold start because providers initialize before Application.onCreate (Q182).

questions.promptHtml: What are the implicit broadcast restrictions introduced in Android 8.0, and how do they affect an app that listens for CONNECTIVITY_ACTION or PACKAGE_ADDED in its manifest?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you know that the break was tied to targetSdk 26 and what the supported replacements are.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For apps targeting API 26 or higher, a manifest receiver can no longer receive most implicit broadcasts, meaning those that are not addressed to the app's package or component. There is a short exempt list, such as BOOT_COMPLETED and LOCALE_CHANGED. Everything else I register at runtime while a component is alive, or I switch to a purpose-built API such as ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback or JobScheduler/WorkManager constraints.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Implicit = no explicit component or package target. Explicit broadcasts (setPackage/setComponent) are unaffected.
  • The restriction is per targetSdk: if your app targets 25 it keeps old behavior on an Android 8 device (though background execution limits still apply). With targetSdk 26+ the filter in the system's broadcast queue skips manifest receivers for non-exempt implicit actions.
  • The exemptions are system broadcasts where waking the app is essential and cheap, for example ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED, ACTION_LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, ACTION_LOCALE_CHANGED, ACTION_MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, USB device/accessory attach, and some telephony/SMS and Bluetooth ones. The official list is on developer.android.com ("Implicit broadcast exceptions"); verify there rather than memorize it.
  • Context-registered receivers are not restricted, but they only exist while the process does. In the background the process may be cached or killed, so it is not a wake-up mechanism.
  • CONNECTIVITY_ACTION was also deprecated in API 28 for general use; NetworkCallback (API 21+; registerDefaultNetworkCallback API 24+) is the replacement and works without a manifest entry.
sendBroadcast(implicit)
        |
        +--> context-registered receivers  -> delivered (if alive)
        +--> manifest receivers
              |-- action in exempt list  -> delivered, process started
              |-- otherwise (target >=26) -> skipped

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val cm = getSystemService(ConnectivityManager::class.java)
cm.registerDefaultNetworkCallback(object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
    override fun onAvailable(network: Network) { /* online */ }
    override fun onLost(network: Network) { /* offline */ }
})

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only on an emulator with targetSdk 25 and shipping a receiver that silently never fires after the bump to 26+.
  • Thinking "implicit restrictions" and "background service restrictions" are the same. Different rules, same release.
  • Using PACKAGE_ADDED in a manifest to detect installs; not exempt, and package visibility (Android 11) also hides other packages.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I make a broadcast explicit for my own receiver? → intent.setPackage(packageName) (and the component if needed).
  2. Is BOOT_COMPLETED guaranteed delivery? → No. See Q179.
  3. What replaces a connectivity manifest receiver for deferred work? → A WorkManager/JobScheduler network constraint, which the system evaluates for you.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "implicit broadcasts do not work in manifest after Oreo". Senior says it is targetSdk 26 scoped, names the exempt categories and where to verify them, and proposes NetworkCallback or job constraints instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a targetSdk bump to 26, a "sync on network regained" feature silently stopped for 30% of users. No crash, only a drop in sync-success metrics.

questions.promptHtml: What are the android:exported requirement (Android 12) and the RECEIVER_EXPORTED / RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED requirement for dynamically registered receivers (Android 13/14)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Version-specific platform knowledge that decides whether a targetSdk bump compiles, installs or crashes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If I target API 31+, every activity, service or receiver with an intent filter must declare android:exported explicitly, otherwise the install fails. For context-registered receivers, the RECEIVER_EXPORTED/RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED flags exist from API 33, and when I target API 34+ I must pass one of them for any non-system broadcast or registerReceiver throws SecurityException. I use ContextCompat.registerReceiver so older API levels also work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• API 31 (manifest): before, a component with an <intent-filter> was implicitly exported. That hid accidental exposure, so the default was removed: targeting 31+ with a missing attribute makes the package fail to install (INSTALL_PARSE_FAILED_MANIFEST_MALFORMED / a manifest merger complaint at build time for libraries).
  • API 33 (runtime flag introduced) and API 34 (enforced for target 34+): registerReceiver(receiver, filter, flags). RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED means only the same app (and the system) can deliver; RECEIVER_EXPORTED lets other apps send. A receiver registered only for system broadcasts (e.g. ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED) is exempt from the requirement, but supplying the flag is harmless.
  • ContextCompat.registerReceiver (androidx.core 1.9.0+) back-fills: on older devices it emulates "not exported" by using a signature-level permission derived from your package, so a flag works on all API levels.
  • Exported receivers should be protected by a permission argument or by validating sender data, because any app can send them intents.
Target Manifest component with filter Context receiver
< 31 exported implicit no flags
31-33 exported mandatory flags optional (API 33+)
34+ same flag mandatory for non-system broadcasts

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ContextCompat.registerReceiver(
    context, receiver, IntentFilter("com.example.ACTION_SYNC_DONE"),
    ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED
)
java.lang.SecurityException: com.example: One of RECEIVER_EXPORTED or
RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered
exclusively for system broadcasts

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting exported="true" just to silence the build error; creates an attack surface (Q184).
  • Forgetting third-party libraries: the manifest merger reports their components; fix with tools:node="merge" plus an explicit override only after reading what the component does.
  • Assuming the crash occurs on the OS version, rather than on targetSdk 34.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does my own app's explicit broadcast still need the flag? → The check is on registration, not on sender. Use NOT_EXPORTED for self-broadcasts.
  2. Does exported=false block the system from delivering BOOT_COMPLETED? → The system is exempt from export checks, so a boot receiver is commonly exported=true only for convention; check the target docs, false generally still works for system broadcasts.
  3. How do you audit a large app? → Run the manifest merger report, grep merged AndroidManifest.xml for exported="true", and justify each.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "add exported to every component". Senior separates the install-time (31) and runtime (34) failures, uses ContextCompat for backward compatibility, and treats each exported=true as a security review item.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A targetSdk 34 release crashed on launch for a screen that registered a custom action receiver in onCreate; staging used targetSdk 33 so it passed QA.

questions.promptHtml: Explain ordered, sticky and local broadcasts. Which ones should you still use today?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know old APIs well enough to maintain legacy code and to replace them correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Normal broadcasts go to all receivers in no defined order. Ordered ones (sendOrderedBroadcast) are delivered one receiver at a time by priority, and each can modify the result or abort it. Sticky broadcasts stay cached so late registrants get the last value; sendStickyBroadcast is deprecated since API 21, though reading ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED that way still works. LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated too; in-process events should be a SharedFlow/StateFlow or observable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Ordered: the system maintains a queue; each receiver runs to completion before the next starts. Priority comes from android:priority (-1000..1000) or IntentFilter.setPriority. A receiver can call abortBroadcast(), setResultCode/Data/Extras. Used for e.g. SMS delivery in old Android and for "result receiver" patterns. Because it is serial, one slow receiver delays everyone and hits the timeout (Q178).
  • Sticky: the system keeps the last Intent per action. Anyone calling registerReceiver(null, filter) gets it immediately. Deprecated because it has no permission control (any app can send or modify it). Remaining public sticky broadcasts are sent by the system (battery, dock state), and reading them with a null receiver is the supported one-shot read.
  • Local: LocalBroadcastManager (androidx.localbroadcastmanager) never leaves the process, which is safe, but it is a global static bus with no type safety, and is deprecated (1.1.0).
  • Replacement for in-process events: a singleton MutableSharedFlow collected with repeatOnLifecycle, or a repository exposing a Flow.
// one-shot sticky read, still valid
val status = context.registerReceiver(null, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED))
val pct = status?.let {
    it.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1) * 100 / it.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_SCALE, 100)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Relying on priority across different apps for security: another app can use a higher priority and abort.
  • Using abortBroadcast on a normal (non-ordered) broadcast: throws BroadcastReceiver trying to return result during a non-ordered broadcast.
  • Keeping LocalBroadcastManager for new code because "it is faster": a Flow does the same without a global bus.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is ordering guaranteed between manifest and dynamic receivers? → For ordered, dynamic receivers of equal priority go first, then manifest ones, subject to priority.
  2. How would you replace a LocalBroadcast with a Flow without losing events during rotation? → SharedFlow(replay=0) loses events; use a Channel to a ViewModel (consumed once) or a StateFlow for state.
  3. Why was sticky removed from the public path? → Insecure (no permission), and the cached intent has no lifecycle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can describe each. Senior knows which survive, the security reason for deprecation, the main-thread serial execution of ordered broadcasts, and picks the right Flow primitive for the replacement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legacy ordered broadcast with five internal receivers blocked on one slow disk write and caused sporadic ANRs; replacing the chain with direct function calls removed them.

questions.promptHtml: How long can onReceive run, what does goAsync() change, and what should you do for work that takes longer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Receivers are a classic place to cause main-thread jank and ANRs; shows if you understand the contract.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onReceive runs on the main thread and the broadcast is considered done when it returns. The system budget is on the order of 10 seconds for foreground-priority broadcasts and 60 for background ones, after which an ANR is raised. goAsync() returns a PendingResult so I can finish on another thread, but it does not extend the budget meaningfully. For anything real I enqueue WorkManager or start a foreground service and return immediately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• After onReceive returns, the process may be demoted. The system no longer sees any running component, so a plain Thread you spawned may be killed with the process, even in seconds.
  • goAsync() tells the system "I am not done when onReceive returns", keeping the broadcast open until PendingResult.finish(). The timeout (AOSP BROADCAST_FG_TIMEOUT = 10s, BROADCAST_BG_TIMEOUT = 60s; verify in ActivityManagerConstants) still applies, and exceeding it triggers "Broadcast of Intent ... timeout" ANR.
  • Foreground broadcasts are those sent with FLAG_RECEIVER_FOREGROUND (system uses it for some alarm/boot/time ones).
  • goAsync is for short work (a few hundred ms to a few seconds): parsing a result, writing a small DB row, calling setResult in an ordered broadcast.
  • Coroutine form: launch in a CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default), finally { pending.finish() }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DoneReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val pending = goAsync()
        CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            try {
                saveSmall(context, intent)
            } finally {
                pending.finish() // always, or the broadcast stays open until the system times out
            }
        }
    }
}
// long work: hand off
WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueue(OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>().build())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting finish() on an exception path.
  • Calling goAsync() twice or after returning.
  • Starting a plain background Service from the receiver on Android 8+; may throw IllegalStateException (app in background).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to a bare Thread started in onReceive? → Nothing keeps the process alive; it can be killed mid-work.
  2. Does goAsync give me 10 seconds more? → No; it only defers the completion signal.
  3. How to detect slow receivers in prod? → ANR traces mention BroadcastReceiver.onReceive and Broadcast of Intent; also StrictMode/Perfetto slices.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "do not block onReceive; use goAsync". Senior states the main-thread contract, that goAsync is not an extension, the timeout values and the right hand-off (WorkManager/FGS).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An alarm receiver parsed a 2 MB JSON on the main thread; p95 onReceive was 4 s on low-end devices and ANR rate rose 0.3%.

questions.contextHtml:
A reminders app (800k DAU, 70% Samsung/Xiaomi/Oppo) re-schedules alarms in a receiver on BOOT_COMPLETED. After the release that targets API 34, support tickets say reminders vanish after reboot for about 12% of users. The manifest is below, there is no crash. Logcat on a Pixel emulator shows the receiver fires; on a Xiaomi test phone it never does.

<receiver android:name=".BootReceiver">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/>
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>

The receiver reads credentials from credential-encrypted storage and calls AlarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle.
questions.promptHtml: Why might the boot broadcast not work for these users and how would you fix and verify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the permission" or "OEM bug, nothing to do". Misses the several independent causes (stopped state, direct boot, exact alarm permission, OEM autostart) and offers no verification method.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 12% clustered by OEM or by Android version? (OEM autostart vs platform behaviour.) Does it fail for users who never opened the app after install or after force-stop? (stopped state.) Do affected users have a lock screen? (credential-encrypted storage unavailable before unlock.) Is SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM granted? (targetSdk 33/34 changes.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-schedule all alarms also on every app foreground and via a daily periodic WorkManager job as a safety net; ship a server-side "missed reminder" push as fallback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Missing <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/> (manifest above has no permission shown; without it the broadcast never arrives, normal permission, granted at install).
    • OEM autostart/background-run restriction blocks the receiver on Xiaomi/Oppo (not part of AOSP).
    • App in the stopped state (force-stopped by user or "clean" tool) gets no broadcasts until user launches it.
    • Direct boot: if the receiver is directBootAware it gets LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED before unlock, and credential-encrypted storage throws; the normal BOOT_COMPLETED arrives only after unlock.
    • setExactAndAllowWhileIdle throws SecurityException without exact-alarm access on 14+ (for SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, default-denied for new installs targeting 33+), killing the receiver silently in a swallowed try/catch.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> | grep -i permission; reboot the emulator and run adb logcat -b all | grep BootReceiver; adb shell cmd package set-stopped-state (or am force-stop) then adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED -p <pkg> to simulate; adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep <pkg> to check alarms are actually scheduled; test on a physical Xiaomi with autostart off.
  5. Root cause: Typically several: no permission/or stopped state and OEM autostart. In a case like this, the manifest was missing the permission, plus alarms failing the exact-alarm check.
  6. Fix: Short-term: add the permission; wrap scheduling with canScheduleExactAlarms() and fall back to setAndAllowWhileIdle; do not touch credential storage on LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED, use device-protected storage for the minimal data needed. Long-term: persist schedules in Room, treat boot as one of several triggers.
  7. Prevention: instrumentation test using adb shell am broadcast in CI, a metric "alarms rescheduled after boot", device-farm run on OEM devices.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not request battery-optimization exemption just for this (Play policy and user annoyance); I would not use a persistent foreground service to survive; it does not fix a missing broadcast. On Android 15, BOOT_COMPLETED receivers also cannot launch certain foreground service types (e.g. dataSync, mediaPlayback), so I would not start a service from here.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user installed the app and never opened it. → No boot broadcast: apps are in the stopped state until first user launch.
  • Can I use LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED? → Only with android:directBootAware="true" and device-protected storage; good for alarms, bad for anything needing user credentials.
  • Android 15 target: what changes? → Restricted FGS types cannot be started from a boot receiver; verify exact list on developer.android.com.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite alarm app had perfect numbers on Pixels. The real loss was a flurry of cleaner apps force-stopping it nightly; we stopped trusting boot as the only trigger and added a re-arm on every launch and a WorkManager heartbeat.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames OEMs, no verification plan.
  • Hire: names permission, stopped state and direct boot, and uses adb to test.
  • Strong hire: also covers exact alarm access, Android 15 FGS-from-boot limit, redundancy design and metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you share a file:// URI with another app on modern Android, and how does FileProvider solve it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Sharing a photo or PDF is a routine task; wrong answers cause crashes or data leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since API 24, passing a file:// URI outside the app throws FileUriExposedException for apps targeting 24+, because the receiver would need raw filesystem access to my private storage. FileProvider is a ContentProvider subclass that maps a file to a content:// URI and lets me grant temporary read/write permission to just the receiving app via FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Private files (filesDir, cacheDir) are owned by my UID with mode 0700 directories, so another app cannot open the path even if it knows it. A content URI makes my process open the file and hand a ParcelFileDescriptor over Binder. Access is per URI, temporary, and revoked when the receiving task finishes or the device reboots, or explicitly via revokeUriPermission.

Setup has three parts:

  1. Manifest <provider> with exported="false" and grantUriPermissions="true".
  2. An XML resource declaring which directories may be shared (logical names, not real paths).
  3. FileProvider.getUriForFile(context, authority, file).
<provider
    android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.fileprovider"
    android:exported="false"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data
        android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
        android:resource="@xml/file_paths"/>
</provider>
<!-- res/xml/file_paths.xml -->
<paths>
    <cache-path name="shared_images" path="images/"/>
</paths>

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val file = File(cacheDir, "images/receipt.png")
val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(this, "$packageName.fileprovider", file)
val send = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
    type = "image/png"
    putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
}
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(send, null))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Missing FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION: receiver gets SecurityException: Permission Denial: opening provider.
  • File path not covered by any <paths> entry: IllegalArgumentException: Failed to find configured root that contains /data/....
  • Authority mismatch between manifest and getUriForFile (hard-coded vs applicationId).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is ClipData needed for? → Grants from startActivity are applied to URIs in getData() and getClipData(); for EXTRA_STREAM on ACTION_SEND the framework copies it into ClipData, but with custom extras you must set setClipData yourself.
  2. Why exported=false yet others can read? → Access comes from a URI grant, not from export.
  3. How long does the grant last? → Until the receiving component's task is finished or the device restarts, unless persisted (takePersistableUriPermission for SAF URIs; not for FileProvider).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can copy the setup. Senior explains the UID/filesystem reason, grant lifetime, ClipData behaviour, and which <paths> roots are safe (see Q181).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster Failed to find configured root appeared only for users who had moved the app to external storage on old devices; the files-path entry did not cover getExternalFilesDir.

questions.contextHtml:
A security scan of a banking-lite app (1.2M MAU) flags that another installed app can read internal files. The team uses FileProvider to share statement PDFs. Code review finds:

<provider
    android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="com.bank.lite.fp"
    android:exported="true"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
               android:resource="@xml/paths"/>
</provider>
<paths>
    <root-path name="all" path="."/>
</paths>

and

fun shareStatement(ctx: Context, name: String) {
    val f = File(ctx.filesDir, "statements/$name")      // name comes from a deep link query param
    val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(ctx, "com.bank.lite.fp", f)
    ctx.startActivity(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri).addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION))
}

Logcat on a test device shows: java.lang.SecurityException: Provider must not be exported on API 34 after a FileProvider update.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how would an attacker exploit it, and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set exported to false" only. Misses that root-path exposes the whole filesystem to any URI grant and that the file name is attacker-controlled (path traversal) so a malicious deep link can obtain a grant to the app's databases or tokens.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which entry points feed name (deep link, intent extra, push)? Is the Intent sent to a fixed receiver or a chooser? Are databases and shared preferences under filesDir? What is the minimum Android version supported?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix with exported="false", remove root-path, and canonicalize the path. Flag the previous build to force-update.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) provider exported (FileProvider throws SecurityException if exported, which also explains the logcat); (b) overly broad root-path; (c) name allows ../ traversal out of statements/; (d) ACTION_VIEW with a grant sent via implicit Intent to any app.
  4. How I'd verify each: Inspect merged manifest in the APK Analyzer; adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> for exported providers; write a test calling shareStatement(ctx, "../../databases/app.db") and assert it throws; test with a malicious app sending a deep link; run Android Lint (ExportedContentProvider, security checks).
  5. Root cause: Misuse of the permission model: sharing is meant to be per-URI via grants, but the path definition included the whole root and the file name was untrusted, so the grant can cover any file the app process can open, including the SQLite DB.
  6. Fix: Short-term: exported="false", <files-path name="statements" path="statements/"/>; validate name against a regex ([A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.pdf) and check f.canonicalPath.startsWith(File(filesDir,"statements").canonicalPath + File.separator). Long-term: share a copy from a dedicated cache/share/ folder and delete it afterwards; target the intent with setPackage or use createChooser with a user-selected target.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule, unit test on traversal, security review checklist: no root-path, no external-path unless needed, exported=false.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not rely on obscurity (random file names) and not use Uri.fromFile. Copying files costs disk and a cleanup job but contains blast radius.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The partner needs the file for 24 hours. → Use takePersistableUriPermission-style flows via SAF (the partner holds the URI), or a short-lived signed download link; FileProvider grants die with the receiving task.
  • Can I protect with a custom permission instead of grants? → For exported providers yes, but FileProvider forbids being exported; write a custom provider only with strong reason.
  • Why did this pass QA? → Functional tests only share your own files; nobody tries other paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a pentest used a crafted deep link to receive a read grant on an app's shared_prefs file containing a refresh token. The fix was three lines plus a rule: external input never reaches File() without canonicalization.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only toggles exported.
  • Hire: removes root-path, validates path, explains grants.
  • Strong hire: explains canonical path check, blast-radius reduction through copies, and adds tests/lint.

questions.promptHtml: In what order do Application.attachBaseContext, ContentProvider onCreate and Application.onCreate run, and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The answer explains startup cost, SDK auto-initialization, and bugs in multi-process apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Application object is created and attachBaseContext runs first, then the system installs all the app's ContentProviders in the process (calling their onCreate), and only then Application.onCreate runs. So providers initialize before my Application code, on the main thread, adding to cold start. Libraries like Firebase and WorkManager used this to self-initialize, and AndroidX App Startup consolidates it in one provider.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In ActivityThread.handleBindApplication (simplified):

1. Create Application instance (class load)
2. Application.attachBaseContext(base)
3. installContentProviders(...)      <- each provider.attachInfo + onCreate()
4. Application.onCreate()
(5. components such as Activity/Service/Receiver created later)

Consequences:

  • ContentProvider.onCreate cannot assume anything set up in Application.onCreate (e.g., DI graph, lateinit singletons). The famous failure: UninitializedPropertyAccessException inside a provider.
  • Each provider adds IPC registration and class loading; 15 libraries with providers (a real pattern with many SDKs) can cost tens to hundreds of ms on low-end devices.
  • android:initOrder (higher first) orders providers within the same process; only meaningful for same-process providers. android:multiprocess and android:process change which process hosts them.
  • Providers with android:process=":remote" initialize in that process only, so each process runs its own Application and providers (see multi-process chunk).
  • androidx.startup.InitializationProvider runs Initializers in dependency order, so one provider replaces N, and you can disable auto-init (tools:node="remove" on the meta-data) and initialize lazily.
  • Instrumentation: in tests, providers are installed before Instrumentation.callApplicationOnCreate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<provider
    android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported="false"
    tools:node="merge">
    <meta-data
        android:name="androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer"
        android:value="androidx.startup"
        tools:node="remove"/>
</provider>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Application.onCreate to set a config that a library provider needs at its own init.
  • Assuming provider init is lazy.
  • Doing disk I/O in ContentProvider.onCreate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you find which providers slow startup? → Perfetto/trace ActivityThread.handleBindApplication with provider.onCreate slices, or adb shell am start -W plus Android Studio startup profiling; dumpsys package <pkg> lists providers.
  2. Can a provider run in a different process before the main one? → Yes if its android:process differs; it starts that process on first access (or at app start if android:process with eager initOrder... verify, since the system starts providers of the main process eagerly, others lazily).
  3. How do you make a library initialize lazily? → Remove its auto-init entry and call init on first use.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says Application first. Senior states the exact order, shows cost on cold start, knows App Startup, and warns that this is the root of "doubled initialization" in multi-process apps.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Removing three SDK providers and initializing them lazily cut cold start p90 from 1.9 s to 1.5 s on a low-end device cohort.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the access control model behind exported providers, FileProvider and the document picker.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An exported provider can require a permission for reading and another for writing, and path-permission can override these per path. Callers who lack the permission can still be granted temporary access to a specific URI if the provider allows grantUriPermissions, either globally or only for <grant-uri-permission> paths. The grant is passed with FLAG_GRANT_READ/WRITE_URI_PERMISSION on an Intent, and the system enforces it on each Binder call.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Enforcement happens in the provider's host process through ContentProvider.Transport: before query() it checks enforceReadPermission, which asks the system whether the caller UID holds the read permission or a URI grant for this exact URI.

Attribute Effect
android:permission single permission for read and write
readPermission / writePermission separate; override permission
<path-permission> per pathPrefix/path/pathPattern rules, most specific wins
grantUriPermissions="true" any URI can be granted
<grant-uri-permission android:pathPrefix=...> only matching URIs can be granted
  • Grants are tied to URI, caller UID and a mode (read/write). Prefix-matching grants (FLAG_GRANT_PREFIX_URI_PERMISSION) extend to children.
  • Persisted grants exist only for document URIs the user picked (takePersistableUriPermission).
  • Inside the provider, getCallingPackage() and checkCallingUriPermission allow extra checks.
  • Dangerous permissions required by the provider are also enforced; an app without the permission gets SecurityException.
  • protectionLevel="signature" custom permissions are the right tool for sharing between your own apps. Declare the permission before use and be careful of permission squatting on old Android (< API 21).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<provider
    android:name=".NotesProvider"
    android:authorities="com.example.notes"
    android:exported="true"
    android:readPermission="com.example.notes.READ"
    android:writePermission="com.example.notes.WRITE">
    <path-permission android:pathPrefix="/public" android:readPermission="android.permission.INTERNET"/>
</provider>
grantUriPermission("com.partner.app", uri, Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
// later
revokeUriPermission(uri, Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a normal permission as protection: any app can request it at install.
  • Giving write via grant when only read was needed.
  • Putting sensitive data in an unprotected exported provider; the Android 4.2+ default no longer protects.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which wins, path-permission or permission? → The path-specific one for matching paths.
  2. How do you share between two of your apps securely? → signature protection level permission or android:sharedUserId (deprecated, avoid).
  3. Can an app that holds a grant forward it? → Not unless the original grant was given with FLAG_GRANT_PERSISTABLE/delegation by the provider owner; generally no.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "set permission in manifest". Senior explains where enforcement happens, per-URI grants, prefix grants and why signature-level permissions matter.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A provider exposed /export for a partner using a normal permission, and a third app read it; moving to signature or short-lived grants closed it.

questions.promptHtml: What are the main security risks of exported components (activities, services, receivers, providers), and how would you audit an app for them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level reviews expect you to find these issues in other people's code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Any exported component is a public API that any installed app can call with attacker-controlled input. Typical bugs are an exported activity that forwards a nested Intent (intent redirection), an exported service acting on unvalidated extras, an exported receiver trusting a sender, and an exported provider with SQL injection or path traversal. I audit the merged manifest, treat each exported=true as a boundary, require a signature permission when a caller is known, and validate every input.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Surfaces and typical failure:

Component Failure
Activity exported with a WebView loading intent.data (JS bridge exposure); forwards getParcelableExtra("next") to startActivity (intent redirection, can reach non-exported components with your identity)
Service does privileged work by action extra without checking caller
Receiver accepts "reset password" style actions; can be spoofed
Provider selection concatenated into SQL; openFile with uri.path into File (traversal); too wide grants

Rules of thumb:

  • Default to exported="false". Library components may add exported through manifest merge, so read the merged manifest.
  • Validate caller: Binder.getCallingUid()/getCallingPackage() for providers/services, signature-level permission, or Activity.getCallingActivity() (only with startActivityForResult). getReferrer() is spoofable.
  • Never trust extras: use type-safe getters and bound ranges; on API 33+ use getParcelableExtra(key, Class) to avoid type confusion.
  • Nested intents: do not launch them directly; check intent.component?.packageName == packageName, strip grant flags, or resolve it to your own activities. Android 12+ PendingIntent mutability rules (see chunk 10) are the sibling issue.
  • Tools: merged manifest, Lint security checks, adb shell dumpsys package <pkg>, drozer, adb shell am start -n against each exported activity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// provider: parameterized query and strict projection
override fun query(uri: Uri, projection: Array<String>?, selection: String?,
                   args: Array<String>?, sort: String?): Cursor? {
    val qb = SQLiteQueryBuilder().apply {
        tables = "notes"
        setStrict(true)                       // API 14+
        setProjectionMap(PROJECTION_MAP)
    }
    return qb.query(db.readableDatabase, projection, selection, args, null, null, sort)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• exported=true added "to make it work" for a deep link; deep links need only the intent filter and an exported activity, so scope the filter and validate data.
  • Believing android:permission of normal protection level secures anything.
  • Trusting Intent.getPackage() from the sender.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is intent redirection? → The exported component launches an attacker-supplied Intent using the app's identity, bypassing export checks of private components.
  2. Does an exported flag on the activity alias matter? → Yes, aliases have their own exported.
  3. How do you let a partner app call my service? → Signature permission if same signer; else allow-list by package and signature digest (PackageManager.checkSignatures/getSigningInfo) then validate calling UID.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "do not export unless needed". Senior lists concrete bug classes per component, validates callers properly, and builds an audit workflow with tooling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An internal audit found three SDK-contributed exported activities; one accepted a URL and loaded it into a WebView with a JS bridge.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app's crash dashboard (2.5M sessions/day) shows two issues after a refactor: IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered: ...ConnectivityFragment$receiver$1 (0.4% of sessions) and LeakCanary reports a leaked MainActivity retained by a ConnectivityFragment. Code:

class ConnectivityFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_conn) {
    private val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { banner.isVisible = !isOnline(c) }
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        requireActivity().registerReceiver(receiver, IntentFilter(ConnectivityManager.CONNECTIVITY_ACTION))
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        requireActivity().unregisterReceiver(receiver)
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

Crash happens mostly on rotation and back navigation; the app targets API 34.
questions.promptHtml: Find all the bugs and give the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch" or "move unregister to onDestroyView". Misses the target 34 flag requirement, the deprecated action, the asymmetric lifecycle, and the activity-scoped registration from a view-scoped callback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the Fragment get detached/re-added (back stack) without onDestroy? Is banner a view binding? Is the crash on all API levels? What does the receiver need to show?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by registering/unregistering in matching callbacks; feature-flag the banner if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) register in onViewCreated (can run many times per Fragment instance, back stack) but unregister in onDestroy (once): registers N times, unregisters once, leaks and, when the Fragment is detached, requireActivity() throws; (b) onDestroy may run after the activity is already gone; (c) the receiver captures banner (a view) so the leaked receiver retains the old view hierarchy and Activity; (d) no RECEIVER_* flag for target 34 and the CONNECTIVITY_ACTION is deprecated since API 28.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log registration counts; Do-not-keep-activities plus rotate; LeakCanary trace shows Activity.mReceivers -> receiver -> Fragment; adb shell dumpsys activity broadcasts or dumpsys activity service to inspect registered receivers; unit test with FragmentScenario moving state to DESTROYED.
  5. Root cause: Registration scoped to the view lifecycle, release scoped to the Fragment, and the receiver is registered on the Activity context, which outlives the Fragment's view.
  6. Fix: Don't use a broadcast at all; use NetworkCallback exposed as a Flow and collect it with viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED). If a receiver must stay, register with ContextCompat.registerReceiver(requireContext(), ..., RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED) in onStart and unregister in onStop.
  7. Prevention: Lint check (UnsafeProtectedBroadcastReceiver, leak detector), architectural rule "no raw receivers in UI", LeakCanary in debug, a lifecycle test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not swallowing IllegalArgumentException: hides the leak. Not moving to the Application context to dodge leaks; it removes the symptom, not the unbounded registrations.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can unregister be called in onDestroyView? → Yes if register is in onViewCreated; this keeps a matched pair.
  • Would DefaultLifecycleObserver help? → Yes, register in onStart and unregister in onStop in one place.
  • Why only some users? → Rotation and back-stack users; others never trigger re-creation.

sections.label: Senior war story
